operations.name: A. J. Muste

expected.name: A. J. Muste
expected.description:
A. J. Muste was a clergyman who moved into labour and peace organising, becoming a central advocate of nonviolent direct action and a bridge between labour militancy and pacifist politics. He led Brookwood Labor College, and worked through the Fellowship of Reconciliation, the War Resisters League, Peacemakers and the Committee for Nonviolent Action. He died in New York City on February 11, 1967, aged 82. (Abraham Johannes Muste, born at Zierikzee in the Netherlands on January 8, 1885)

He was arrested repeatedly across nearly fifty years, and the pattern matters more than any single term: several separate political arrests and short detentions rather than one long sentence.

In February 1919, as spokesman for the striking textile workers at Lawrence, Massachusetts, he was beaten by police and pulled from a picket line, then charged with disturbing the peace and loitering. He was held about a week before eyewitness testimony supported his account and the charges were dismissed. In early September 1931 he was arrested at the Paterson silk strike alongside Norman Thomas and other labour supporters.

On June 15, 1955 he was one of twenty-nine pacifists who refused to take shelter during New York City's compulsory civil-defence drill and stayed above ground in City Hall Park. He was arraigned some nine hours later, bail was set at $1,500 a head, and the group was released within forty-eight hours after supporters raised more than $35,000. They were convicted on December 22, 1955 and their sentences suspended.

His best-documented jail term began on July 1, 1959, when he and other members of Omaha Action crossed the fence at a missile construction site near Mead, Nebraska. He refused bail and stayed in jail until his court appearance on July 9 — eight nights. The judge imposed six months and a $500 fine, then suspended both and placed him on a year's probation conditioned on his staying away from military-base demonstrations. He did not serve six months: later summaries sometimes confuse his suspended sentence with the imprisonment of other Omaha Action defendants.

On April 21, 1966, at eighty-one, he and five other American pacifists tried to demonstrate against the Vietnam War near the United States Embassy in Saigon. South Vietnamese police arrested them, held them in a detention room at the airport and expelled them from the country.

expected.description: Ana Lucia Gelabert was born in central Cuba on July 6, 1938 and returned to the United States in 1961. expected.name: Pam Fadem
expected.description: Pam Fadem (Pamela Fadem) is a white anti-imperialist activist and a founding member of the John Brown Anti-Klan Committee. In 1984, while living in Austin, Texas, she was charged with criminal contempt for resisting a federal grand jury investigating the Puerto Rican independence movement and allied clandestine organizations — part of a wave of subpoenas that targeted John Brown Anti-Klan Committee members and Puerto Rican solidarity activists. Ordered to appear before the grand jury in Brooklyn on February 16, 1984, she went instead to the United Nations to challenge the investigation and was arrested leaving the UN building; after telling the court she would not appear, she was jailed. Convicted of criminal contempt and facing a three-year prison term, she saw sentencing postponed because of her serious medical condition — and on April 19, 1985 Judge Eugene Nickerson, after hearing medical testimony, suspended the prison sentence and placed her on three years of probation. She served only that brief initial detention. Fadem went on to decades of movement work, including as a longtime organizer with the California Coalition for Women Prisoners and its newsletter The Fire Inside, focused on prison abolition, women prisoners' rights, and disability justice.

The original August 23, 1983 Nuclear Resister prints a report credited to Zanzig and Mark Anderlik about their July 10 arrest near Romeo-29, with three visiting activists. expected.description: Leonard J. Cohen was a staff member of the UFO Coffeehouse, an antiwar gathering place used by soldiers stationed at Fort Jackson in Columbia, South Carolina. expected.body:
Richmond Five prosecution

Albert Moore helped organize the Black Community Information Center in Richmond, Virginia, with his brother Howard. FBI agents arrested him in early April 1971 in the Richmond Five weapons prosecution. Contemporary reporting records a conviction for transporting stolen weapons across state lines and acquittal on the conspiracy count. The Party denounced the case as an attack on Black community organizing. His exact custody duration and release date remain unverified.

The Militant reported that Jacob Bethea, Charles Brunson, Albert Moore and Howard Moore were sentenced on September 10, 1971 following convictions that summer. Its four-to-eight-year range describes the group, not a verified individual term or time actually served.

The political-targeting and informant allegations come from contemporary defense reporting and are attributed to that reporting; they are not presented as judicial findings. The Moore brothers are identified with the Richmond Information Center, without assuming Black Panther Party membership. The documented historical case does not establish present-day custody.

Sources

  • The Black Panther, July 19, 1971, printed pages 5 and 15: Richmond Five arrests and trial outcomes
  • The Militant, October 8, 1971, printed page 2: subsequent convictions and September 10 sentencing
